SOCs depend on Level 1 analysts for alert triage under growing alert volumes, alert fatigue, and tool fragmentation, which opens windows for lateral movement and exfiltration before response starts (§1, p. 2). LLM-based multi-agent systems using MCP are being adopted to automate these Level 1 tasks, but their autonomy and tool access expose attack classes with no direct analog in traditional software security — tool poisoning, tool shadowing, indirect prompt injection, memory poisoning, inter-agent trust exploitation, and confused deputy attacks (Abstract, p. 1; §1, p. 2). Existing taxonomies (OWASP LLM/Agentic Top 10, OWASP MCP Top 10, MITRE ATLAS, ATFAA) systematize these risks but offer no consensus mechanism to translate them into deployable middleware controls, and no prior work combines a functional multi-agent SOC architecture on a real SIEM with a systematically derived, experimentally validated security framework (§1, pp. 2-3; Table 1, pp. 4-5).

A security framework for MCP-based multi-agent SOC pipelines, implemented as a middleware gateway interposed between agents and MCP servers, through which no agent can invoke any tool directly (§3.2, p. 7). It comprises a connection-phase tool registration validator (description regex scan, namespace-ownership anti-shadowing check, SHA-256 manifest pinning against rug-pull; §3.2.1, p. 8) plus five execution layers: L1 runtime RBAC, L2 rate limiting (20-30 calls/60 s per role; 10 approval requests/hour against oversight saturation and consent fatigue), L3 input validation (JSON Schema + injection scans on tool arguments, inter-agent handoffs, memory context with per-session namespacing, and external data), L4 output validation (injection/exfiltration/self-propagation patterns, 100 KB size cap), and L5 append-only audit log with SHA-256 hashing of sensitive fields (§3.2.2-3.2.6, pp. 9-12), plus transversal controls (failure opacity, version pinning, session UUIDs, supply-chain binary hashing, channel authentication; §3.2.7, p. 12). The protected agentic system is a sequential three-agent triage-enrichment-response pipeline (GPT-4o mini agents with role-specialized allowlists over 16 Wazuh tools: 3 triage, 7 enrichment, 6 response) with persistent shared memory, connected to a real Wazuh SIEM through a custom MCP server; the response agent never executes actions directly — it produces a structured plan with human approval and escalation flags (HITL), and propose_wazuh_rule only returns a proposal for analyst review (§3.1, pp. 5-6).

Design-and-experimental-validation study: (i) threat model of 35 attack vectors selected from five taxonomies under explicit architectural-relevance, empirical-grounding, and SOC-applicability inclusion rules, of which 29 are middleware-addressable and covered (§3.2.8, pp. 12-13; Table 2, p. 13); (ii) laboratory implementation in Python 3.11/FastAPI with GPT-4o mini (temperature 0.1), a Rust Wazuh MCP server (Streamable HTTP, MCP 2025-06-18), Wazuh 4.14.0 on Vagrant, and Docker Compose with three isolated network segments (§3.3, pp. 15-17; Table 4, p. 17); (iii) controlled evaluation via a purpose-built, specification-compliant malicious MCP server (4 end-to-end attack tools) plus test-harness injections, organized into six suites T00-T05 with 25 unique attack instances repeated N=20 times, yielding 600 block decisions, each paired with legitimate cases for the false-block metric (§3.4-3.5, pp. 18-23; Table 5, p. 20); complemented by a full-pipeline demonstration under unprotected vs. secured conditions (§4.2, pp. 23-24), per-control micro-benchmarks (N=10,000; §4.3, p. 24), an obfuscation-robustness probe (§4.4, p. 25), and a false-positive probe on attack-like benign SOC traffic (§4.5, pp. 25-26). Design alignment is externally checked against the OWASP Practical Guide for Secure MCP Server Development v1.0 (Table 3, p. 14). Code is openly available (p. 29).

Not specified quantitatively — the paper does not measure MTTD or MTTR and performs no empirical time-to-detect/time-to-respond comparison against a baseline; its motivation invokes triage delay and alert fatigue only qualitatively (§1, p. 2). What is actually measured is security efficacy and overhead of the middleware: 600/600 attack block decisions, 0 bypasses, and 0 false blocks on the evaluated legitimate set across six suites (Table 12, §4.1, p. 23); a full-pipeline demonstration where decision-relevant response-plan fields were identical between unprotected and secured conditions for a real Wazuh alert and a synthetic SSH brute-force alert, i.e., the security layer preserves benign operational output (§4.2, pp. 23-24); and per-call processing cost below 0.6 ms (below 30 µs with schema precompilation), three to four orders of magnitude smaller than one LLM invocation, so the protection adds negligible latency to the automated triage-enrichment-response loop (Table 13, §4.3, p. 24). Counter-evidence bounding the result: all four obfuscation techniques fully evade the lexical L3/L4 scans (Table 14, §4.4, p. 25) and 7 of 8 attack-like benign SOC inputs are falsely blocked by the isolated L3 argument scan (Table 15, §4.5, pp. 25-26).

Field: General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Agent Systems
Extraction: First work to jointly deliver a functional multi-agent SOC architecture, MCP integration, an implemented middleware security framework, and experimental evaluation against controlled attacks — no reviewed prior work satisfies all four dimensions (Table 1, §2, pp. 4-5). It demonstrates that systematic middleware controls can secure MCP-based agentic deployments without modifying agents, models, or MCP servers, treating the LLM as a black box (Abstract, p. 1; §3.3, p. 16; §5, p. 26), and operationalizes recurrent design principles of the agentic-SOC literature (role specialization with least privilege, persistent shared memory, trust-boundary enforcement, HITL oversight; §2, p. 3). It shows pre-admission inspection of tool metadata is implementable and effective against tool poisoning and name collision (§5, p. 26), argues deterministic (non-LLM) security decisions preserve reproducibility and avoid reintroducing the prompt-injection surface (§3.2, p. 8), and offers a portability recipe for other linear agent pipelines via four configuration points (§3.3, p. 17). Controls map onto the OWASP secure-MCP guidance (Table 3, p. 14) and the full stack is open-sourced (p. 29).

The blocking guarantee holds only for non-adaptive, in-clear payloads: all four obfuscation techniques (base64, Cyrillic homoglyphs, Spanish translation, paraphrase) completely evade the lexical L3 scan, and the two L4-detectable payloads are likewise evaded (§4.4, Table 14, p. 25); conversely, 7/8 benign attack-like SOC inputs (shell logs, file paths, tickets quoting attackers) are false positives of the isolated argument scan, so lexical matching is imprecise in both directions (§4.5, Table 15, pp. 25-26; §5, p. 27). Adaptive adversaries were not modeled and failure opacity is verified only structurally (§5, p. 26). Six of 35 vectors remain uncovered (RAG poisoning, adversarial embeddings, package hallucination out of middleware scope; consensus manipulation and covert coordination inapplicable to the sequential topology; replay requires server-side freshness checks) (§3.2.8, p. 13; §5, p. 27). The DNS-rebinding origin check was inactive in the evaluated deployment, compensated by loopback binding and network segmentation (§3.2.7, p. 12; §5, p. 27). Evaluation used a single LLM (GPT-4o mini) and a file-based memory store unsuitable for production scale (§5, p. 27). Future work: semantic/classifier/LLM-based detection (primary avenue), extension to non-sequential topologies via a transition-graph handoff validator, cross-model evaluation, production-grade deployment with SIEM-integrated audit log and real-time anomaly detection, tamper-evident hash-chained logging, and periodic re-application of the vector-selection methodology (§6, pp. 28-29).

Directly relevant as the security-enablement layer for the thesis object (an agentic copilot reducing MTTD/MTTR in incident response): it is built on exactly the target scenario — LLM multi-agent triage-enrichment-response automation of SOC Level 1 work on a real SIEM, motivated by alert fatigue and response delay (§1, p. 2; §3.1, p. 5) — and answers the adoption-blocking question of how to deploy such a copilot safely, showing the guardrail layer preserves benign operational output and adds sub-millisecond overhead (§4.2-4.3, pp. 23-24). Its HITL design (response agent proposes, never executes; approval rate-limiting against consent fatigue) is a concrete pattern for the 'copilot' rather than 'autopilot' posture the thesis argues for (§3.1, p. 6; §3.2.3, p. 9). It does not, however, provide MTTD/MTTR evidence, so in the synthesis it supports the feasibility/trust dimension (RQ on architectures and safeguards) rather than the quantitative benefit dimension. P94 was the only unqualified 'Include' of RSL cycle 3.

High — it is squarely in-domain (agentic multi-agent AI automating SOC incident triage-enrichment-response over a real SIEM) and uniquely combines architecture, MCP integration, and experimental validation (Table 1, pp. 4-5), making it a cornerstone for the thesis chapters on copilot architecture and deployment safeguards; the absence of MTTD/MTTR quantification is its only gap for the review's primary outcome.
